summary_html: A **judge orders** CPS to investigate or assess during civil/criminal proceedings. Federal funding statutes (ASFA/IV-E) tether court findings to child-welfare actions, embedding judicial oversight into intake-to-case flow.
authority_html:
- **ASFA (42 U.S.C. §§ 671–675)** — court ‘reasonable efforts’ findings; permanency timelines  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funding structure linking court oversight to agency actions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that chapter XIIA gives the probate court broad authority to enter orders affecting adults, including an order requiring a parent to leave the home, where such orders are necessary for the well-being of a child within the court's jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: A court that has jurisdiction over a child may direct adults in the household, which is the statutory basis for judicially initiated protective action.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the Legislature has conferred very broad authority to the probate court

key_cases.holding: The Court held the family court's ex parte and referee proceedings authorizing withdrawal of an infant's life support were fatally defective, that inadequate notice to a respondent is a jurisdictional defect, and it set out the notice, evidentiary and decision-maker standards such a case requires.
key_cases.relevance: A judicially initiated protective proceeding is void as to a parent who was never properly notified, no matter how urgent the medical situation.
key_cases.quote: The absence of this notice to a respondent in a protective proceeding constitutes a jurisdictional defect.

key_cases.holding: The Court held Michigan's one-parent doctrine unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment, so a court may not enter dispositional orders infringing a parent's rights until that parent has been individually adjudicated unfit, and overruled In re CR.
key_cases.relevance: A judicially ordered CPS referral or petition against only one parent cannot by itself authorize orders against the other parent, who is entitled to his or her own adjudication.
key_cases.quote: due process requires a specific adjudication of a parent's unfitness before the state can infringe the constitutionally protected parent-child relationship

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of an unadjudicated father's parental rights, holding that the court rules do not require the agency to plead and prove an adjudication against every parent before the family court may act in its dispositional capacity — the one-parent doctrine the Michigan Supreme Court held unconstitutional in In re Sanders (2014).
key_cases.relevance: OVERRULED BY IN RE SANDERS (2014): CR is the origin of Michigan's one-parent doctrine, under which jurisdiction over the child was thought to authorize orders against a parent who had never been adjudicated.
key_cases.quote: making it possible, under the proper circumstances, to terminate parental rights even of a parent who, for one reason or another, has not participated in the protective proceeding

search_keywords: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, dentists, physician's assistants, registered dental hygienists, medical examiners, nurses, and persons licensed to provide emergency medical care — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(a)
Audiologists, psychologists, physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, and athletic trainers

Marriage and family therapists, licensed professional counselors, social workers, licensed master's social workers, licensed bachelor's social workers, registered social service technicians, and social service technicians
Persons employed in a professional capacity in any office of the friend of the court
School administrators, school counselors, and teachers

MDHHS eligibility specialists, family independence managers, family independence specialists, social services specialists, social work specialists, social work specialist managers, and welfare services specialists — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(b)
Employees of an organization that federal funding statutes, regulations, or contracts would otherwise bar from reporting absent a state mandate — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(c)
Not universal: any other person, including a child, MAY report but is not required to — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624
reporting_details: Michigan is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals and MDHHS employees listed in Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1) must report, and they must report immediately to MDHHS centralized intake by telephone or through the Michigan Online Reporting System. A telephone report must be followed within 72 hours by a written report on form DHS-3200, faxed or emailed to Centralized Intake; a report filed through the online reporting system that contains the information required by Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(2) counts as the written report, and MDHHS states that reporting online eliminates the requirement to fill out a DHS-3200 form. Any other person may report voluntarily under Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: MDHHS centralized intake receives the report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.628(1) requires the department, within 24 hours of receiving a report, to refer it to the prosecuting attorney and local law enforcement or to commence an investigation.
Not specified; MDHHS states CPS has 30 days to complete an investigation unless extenuating circumstances require an extension.
